versions.analysis_for_next: Version 0 over-predicts the polar labels. Neutral recall is poor: 26 neutral texts went to positive and 23 to negative, while positive and negative recall are fairly good. Patterns behind the errors: (1) Neutral texts went to positive when they mention plans or events: going to a game or movie, 'the move tomorrow', requests to a celebrity, fan hype, promos, a ':)' or '<3'. Annotators treat these as neutral unless the author states strong enthusiasm. (2) Neutral texts went to negative for mild personal grumbling or self-mockery ('I'm dead', 'lmao', a paper due, a long workday), for joking sports commentary, and for reported criticism of public figures or companies in headline-like text. (3) Condolences, prayers and RIP wishes are gold positive (supportive), yet the model called them negative. (4) Some headlines about wins and achievements are gold positive, and headlines about attacks, deficits or deaths are gold negative, so news is not always neutral. These cases are noisier, so I will only nudge here. Changes: neutral now explicitly covers plans, requests and mild hype or grumbling without strong explicit emotion. Positive requires clear enthusiasm, praise, celebration of wins, or sympathy and prayers. Negative requires strong explicit negative feeling or clearly bad events such as attacks or deaths. The polar thresholds are raised overall.

Version 1 overcorrected. Raising the bar for the polar labels pushed 47 gold-positive and 41 gold-negative texts into neutral, and macro-F1 fell from 72 to 68. Neutral recall rose to 96 of 108, but that does not make up for the losses. The annotators label mild cues as polar. Positive includes event promotions and invites ('come join us', 'get your tickets', 'come support'), eager plans ('for sure going to', 'can't I just fast forward to'), hopes ('I hope', ':D'), fun or treat framing, and approving reports of wins. Negative includes mild personal complaints ('going to die', 'not in the state of mind', 'I miss', ':-/', 'so long from now'), disapproving remarks or sarcasm about public figures, and news about harm (deficit, bombing, funeral, vandals, injury). Neutral is mostly pure information, questions, speculation or ambiguous banter with no evaluative slant. Plan: go back to the lower polar threshold of version 0 and keep the condolences-are-positive rule. Neutral is now reserved for texts that have no evaluative slant at all, rather than being the default under uncertainty. For mixed tweets, the final or dominant feeling decides.

Version 0 had the best balance (F1 72). Version 1 pushed too much into neutral (F1 68). Version 2 pushed too much into the polar labels: neutral recall fell to 41 of 108, with 39 neutral texts called positive and 28 called negative. The annotators sit between these extremes. The neutral texts that version 2 got wrong fall into four groups. (1) Informational event or promo notices and casual plans ('X is the move tomorrow', 'going to the game Friday', a sign-up, a meeting). (2) Wry jokes or ironic sports and celebrity commentary ('could be worse', 'didn't get the memo', 'implode'). (3) Hyperbolic slang and self-deprecating grumbles ('I'm dead', 'lmao', a paper due, a long shift, 'not ready for this album'). (4) Headlines that report someone else's criticism or a speculative development. The texts version 2 still got right as polar have explicit emotion words, clear praise or insults, or eager markers ('can't wait', 'hyped', 'love', 'come support'). Plan: return to version 0's structure with a moderate threshold and say explicitly that these four groups are neutral. Keep the rules that condolences and prayers are positive and that news of attacks or deaths is negative. For mixed tweets, the dominant feeling decides.

Version 3 is the best so far (F1 75.3) and is fairly balanced. Most remaining errors are polar texts predicted neutral: 26 negative and 21 positive. Fixable patterns: (1) Headlines about harmful events are gold negative, but neutral was predicted: a budget deficit, a missile strike, a funeral, a terrorist charge, a phone that may break, an injury. (2) Sports results stating a win or title are gold positive ('beats', 'won the title'), as are giveaways or ticket pushes ('get your tickets now', 'who wants tickets'). (3) Pointed, skeptical or sarcastic digs at public figures or arguments are gold negative ('someone should have told...', 'why did they...', 'it wouldn't and doesn't'). So are dread about upcoming tasks ('going to die' about a long class day, 'not in the state of mind'), nostalgic 'I miss', and grudging remarks ('not cause I enjoy it'). (4) Calm but clear enjoyment ('perfect friday night', 'for sure going to watch', 'reread for the 7th time') is gold positive. I will add these cues carefully while keeping version 3's neutral list: informational notices, casual plans, wry jokes, laughing 'I'm dead' or 'lmao', and reported criticism in headlines. The neutral tie-breaker becomes slightly weaker. Mixed tweets keep the dominant feeling.

Version 4 is the best so far (F1 77.6), with strong positive and negative recall. Neutral recall dropped to 67, with 24 neutral texts called negative and 17 called positive. Recurring neutral-gold patterns: (1) Wry or ironic commentary on athletes' performances, campaigns or companies ('implode', 'could be worse', 'clear as mud', 'padding his numbers'). These are commentary, not hostility. (2) Minor personal mishaps told matter-of-factly or apologetically ('computer is broke', 'the wrong track played', a long work shift, 'lmao', 'I'm dead'). (3) Fangirl overwhelm ('not ready for this album', 'can't handle'), which is excitement rather than negativity. (4) Pleas or requests to celebrities and fan campaigns ('we want you in X!!!', 'please sing at my wedding <3', 'let's go trending'). (5) Headlines that merely report criticism ('worst offense', 'disliked company'). Plan: keep version 4's structure and add these items to neutral. I will also narrow 'pointed digs' in negative to clear contempt or mockery, so wry commentary stays neutral. The positive and negative cues that recovered recall in version 4 stay unchanged.

Version 5 is the best so far (F1 78.6). The remaining errors are largely noisy or contradictory: slang 'sick' meaning great is gold negative, and one match-win headline is gold positive while another is gold neutral. One consistent fixable pattern is left. Wry sports commentary on a player's poor play ('implode', 'could be worse', 'padding his numbers', 'didn't get the memo') is still predicted negative, but annotators call it neutral. Self-deprecating rhetorical questions ('why did I just...') and mild self-mocking procrastination are also gold neutral. Opinion headlines about companies or politicians that merely report criticism keep drifting to negative. Plan: keep version 5 essentially intact, since its balance is good, and make the neutral list more explicit about sports banter and self-deprecating questions. The negative wording on contempt stays. Small, careful edits only.

Version 6 is the best so far (F1 79.5). The remaining errors are mostly noisy or contradictory (slang 'sick', mixed win headlines, sarcasm labelled positive), so only light, low-risk tweaks make sense. Recurring neutral-gold texts that are still called positive: live game updates told with exclamation ('beating #3 in the 4th quarter', 'defeats X, through to the next round'), meme jokes (Chuck Norris style), 'now watching... hooked' status updates, and comparative political opinions ('more comfortable than Jeb'). Neutral-gold texts still called negative: the laughing 'I'm dead' and headlines that mention a bad reputation. Plan: keep version 6 and add to neutral live score updates, meme jokes, 'now watching' status and hedged comparisons of candidates. The positive rule on wins stays, limited to titles, finals and historic moments, so routine round results go to neutral. Everything else is unchanged to protect the current balance.

Version 7 is the best so far (F1 79.8), but only slightly above version 6. The remaining errors are mostly label noise: slang 'sick' gold negative, sarcasm gold positive, cryptic or garbled texts, and contradictory win headlines. Some low-risk fixes remain. A festive promo inviting people to 'come celebrate' with freebies fell just short of positive (0.48), so celebratory promo language can join positive while dry info sessions stay neutral. A product-defect headline was nearly negative (0.47), so I will name 'may break' style warnings. The fan-campaign and plea texts ('we want you in...', 'please sing at my wedding <3') are still called positive. I will stress that requests or wishes addressed to celebrities are neutral unless they contain explicit praise or excitement words. Everything else stays to preserve the balance.

Version 8 is the best so far (F1 80.8). The remaining errors are mostly noise: sarcasm gold positive, slang 'sick' gold negative, garbled or cryptic texts, and mixed tweets labelled by the first clause. Low-risk tweaks only. (1) A headline about a player reaching a final is gold positive but still predicted neutral, so I will name 'reaches final' and 'beats X to reach' explicitly alongside titles. (2) An author promoting their own show or event with 'please share!!!' is gold positive but predicted neutral, so self-promotion with an eager call to share or come joins positive. Dry info sessions stay neutral. (3) 'computer is broke', told apologetically, is still called negative. I will mention apologetic updates under neutral. Everything else stays to protect the balance.

Version 9 fell from 80.8 to 79.5. Its additions ('please share!!!' self-promotion, 'reaching a final', apologetic updates) fixed nothing. The texts they targeted stayed wrong, and a few neutral texts flipped to positive: a radio-show notice with '!' and a 'coolest console' question. The rest of the change is noise. With only one version left, the safest choice is to return to version 8, the best-performing wording, unchanged. Its balance between neutral and the polar labels has proven best across iterations, and the remaining errors are largely label noise that further tuning cannot fix reliably.
